stem: A histogram is drawn for a frequency distribution. The class intervals are of equal width. Which of the following correctly describes what the height of each bar in the histogram represents?

options.text: The relative frequency multiplied by the class width
The cumulative frequency up to that class
The class mark of that interval

per_option_rationale.rationale: When class widths are equal, height = frequency directly, so each bar height gives the count for that class.
Relative frequency times class width equals the area of the bar in a frequency density histogram, not the height when widths are equal.
Cumulative frequency is plotted in an ogive, not as bar heights in a histogram.
The class mark (midpoint) labels the x-axis position of each bar but is not the bar height.

explanation: For equal class widths, bar height in a histogram equals the class frequency. The area of each bar (height x width) equals frequency; when widths are equal, height alone carries the frequency.

explanation_sections.punchline: Equal-width histogram: height = frequency, because area = frequency x width and width is constant.
explanation_sections.approach: Identify the quantity represented: height encodes frequency when widths are equal; frequency density (frequency/width) is used only for unequal widths. Cumulative frequency is the ogive's quantity.
explanation_sections.lesson: Histogram bar height = frequency only when all class widths are equal; otherwise use frequency density.
explanation_sections.timing: 45 s. Recall the definition and eliminate: ogive for cumulative, class mark is a label, not height.
